headline: Over 200 migrants rescued off Greece coast, mostly from Bangladesh and Sudan
summary: More than 200 irregular migrants, predominantly from Bangladesh and Sudan, were rescued by Greek authorities after crossing the Mediterranean Sea by boat. They arrived on the island of Crete, facing increasing pressure on local facilities.
details: Greek authorities have rescued over 200 irregular migrants attempting to cross the Mediterranean Sea by boat to the coast of Greece. The majority of those rescued are citizens of Bangladesh and Sudan, with some Egyptians also among them.

The arrival of irregular migrants by boat to the southern Greek island of Crete continues, with at least 202 individuals reaching Crete in successive boat journeys from Libya in less than 48 hours, according to Greek newspaper Demokratiya.
This influx of migrants has significantly increased pressure on the island's local authorities and existing migrant reception centers, which are already struggling with rising numbers.
On Thursday morning, a new boat carrying 40 migrants arrived in Ierapetra, southeastern Crete, after being identified by a Frontex aircraft. This was part of a series of arrivals.
With assistance from a coast guard patrol vessel and a fishing boat, the migrants were brought to Ierapetra port for registration and identity verification.

Hours earlier, 112 migrants had arrived on two other boats. The first boat carried 56 people, including 31 Sudanese and 25 Bangladeshi nationals. The second boat also had 56 migrants, comprising 47 Bangladeshis and nine Egyptians.
All rescued migrants are currently housed in a temporary shelter at Heraklion port. This facility is accommodating the new arrivals as the number of migrants on Crete continues to grow.

headline_marked: [[AI model creates 16 new viruses]] never before seen in nature, Stanford study reveals
headline: AI model creates 16 new viruses never before seen in nature, Stanford study reveals
summary: The AI, trained on millions of genomes, designed thousands of new genetic sequences, 16 of which proved to be functional viruses capable of infecting bacteria.
details: Scientists trained an Artificial Intelligence (AI) model to understand how viruses evolve in DNA structure and nature. This AI then used its training to create genetic designs for 16 viruses never before seen in nature.
This groundbreaking information emerged from research conducted by scientists at Stanford University in the United States. The researchers utilized OpenAI's generative AI model 'Evo' for their study.
The model learned various DNA characteristics and evolutionary patterns by analyzing millions of genome data points. Subsequently, it used this knowledge to create thousands of new genome designs.

Scientists then synthesized and tested approximately 300 of these genetic designs in the laboratory. The tests revealed that 16 of them were capable of functioning as effective viruses and could infect bacteria.

The research, published in the science journal 'Science' on Thursday (August 7), stated that 'Evo' was trained from the outset to acquire the ability to design new and effective virus genomes. Just as AI models are trained with vast amounts of text to learn human language, Evo was trained with millions of genetic data points from various branches of life.

Researchers confirm that the genetic characteristics of these newly created viruses do not match any viruses found in nature. This means they are not merely imitations of existing viruses but entirely new genetic designs created by AI.

However, the study did not use genetic information of any pathogens that cause disease in humans during training. Consequently, researchers have stated that the created viruses are not capable of infecting humans.

Nevertheless, the research findings have further intensified scientists' long-standing concerns about the misuse of AI. Specifically, new discussions have begun regarding whether such technology could be used in the future to create harmful pathogens or biological weapons for humans.

At the same time, this technology also holds potential benefits. Scientists believe that the ability to create new viruses as needed could bring significant advancements in treating dangerous antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

Currently, researchers largely depend on finding naturally occurring viruses that can attack specific bacteria. But with the help of AI, new types of treatment methods could emerge if viruses can be custom-designed to target specific bacteria in the future.

However, biosafety experts, public health officials, and synthetic biologists have expressed concern about the risks posed by the rapid advancement of AI in the field of biology. In a commentary accompanying the 'Science' publication, biosafety experts Dr. Thomas Inglesby and Dr. Moritz Hanke from the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security warned that the Stanford research indicates AI is now moving towards the capability of creating dangerous biological weapons.

They argue that the use of similar generative technologies for pathogens that can infect humans, animals, and agricultural crops should be banned in the future. They also called for the creation of strict laws and regulatory frameworks on this matter.

Hanke stated in an interview with The New York Times that if genome-based AI is asked to 'create an influenza genome that spreads faster or is more lethal,' such risks could arise in the future. However, not everyone is so pessimistic.

Professor Tom Ellis of Synthetic Genome Engineering at Imperial College London believes that creating harmful biological weapons will not be so easy. According to him, the viruses created by Evo are extremely small and relatively simple in terms of size and genetic structure. Therefore, some general restrictions on access to genetic information could significantly reduce major risks.
